result.reason: The passage is precisely the Rav Yehuda/Shmuel ruling about writing all property to one's wife making her an apotropos, which is exactly what the 'Wife as Apotropos' section discusses.
The passage poses the question about the minor/infant son ('beno hakatan mah'), which is precisely the topic discussed in the 'Infant Son Case' prose section.
The passage about Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi's ruling regarding a minor son lying in a crib is precisely what the 'Infant Son Case' prose describes and analyzes.

All three items — the obvious cases (son/wife with another as gift vs. apotropos), the obvious cases of betrothed/divorced wife as gift, and the dilemma raised about daughter among sons/wife among brothers/wife among husband's sons — are precisely the 'disputed cases' and preliminary obvious rulings that the 'Disputed Cases' prose section describes in detail.

The passage contains both Ravina's and Rav Avira's opinions in a single Talmudic excerpt, and heading 0 ('Ravina's Resolution') is where the passage should begin, with heading 1 covering Rav Avira's view — but since the text is a single indivisible item containing both opinions, it belongs under heading 0 where Ravina's statement (which comes first in the Gemara) is introduced.

The passage is Rava's dilemma itself — asking whether the apotropos rule applies to a healthy person — which matches heading 0's prose exactly, not the 'Deathbed Context' heading where it currently sits.

The passage discusses exactly the cases of a husband granting his wife the produce/usufruct of his fields and fractional shares of property, and whether she retains her ketubah lien — which is precisely what the 'Produce/Part Gift' section's prose describes.

All six items form a continuous discussion of the 'all property' case: the baraita dispute (Rabbi Eliezer vs. Sages), Rabbi Yehuda the baker's incident (the niece case), the Gemara's inference about healthy vs. deathbed, Rav Avira/Ravina's interpretations, Rav Nachman's ruling, and the question about umdana — all of which are explicitly described in the 'Niece Case' prose section, which covers all of this material in sequence.

The passage presents the baraita about the son presumed dead and both opinions (first opinion that the gift stands, plus Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's dissent and Rav Nachman's ruling), which spans headings 2-4, but the current placement under 'Dead Son Case' is where the baraita is introduced, and since all items must go under one heading, heading 2 is where the baraita text begins and is the best single home for this combined passage.

The passage directly states the Gemara's answer about why the wife's case differs — that it is beneficial to her that the gift be publicized — which is precisely the content described in the 'Wife's Intent' section's prose.

The passage presents the Mishnah about a man distributing property to his sons and giving his wife a small piece of land, then questions why that small grant causes her to lose her ketubah — which is precisely what the 'Distribution Case' prose describes and introduces.

The passage contains all three opinions (Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yosei) together as a single Talmudic unit, and it most naturally belongs under the first heading 'Rav: Active Role' which introduces this sugya, since the essay then breaks down each opinion separately in subsequent sections.
